questions.q: Besides the model weights themselves, what must travel with a handoff to avoid silent underperformance?
options: The chat template used during fine-tuning, since serving the model with a different template than it was trained on causes it to silently underperform
The names of every engineer who worked on the project
The original pretraining dataset in full
The training loss curve image file only
questions.explain: A model fine-tuned with a specific chat template expects inputs formatted that way at inference time. Serving it with a mismatched template degrades quality without necessarily producing an obvious error.

questions.q: Why should eval results be included directly in the handoff package rather than only in a separate report?
options: So the serving team has a concrete baseline of task-specific and general-capability performance to compare against after deployment, making post-launch issues easier to diagnose
Because eval results replace the need for a validated generation config
Eval results are not useful to a serving team under any circumstances
Because serving teams are required by policy to re-run all evaluations themselves
questions.explain: Including eval results, including the general-capability check against a named baseline, gives the serving team a reference point for what 'working correctly' looks like, which helps distinguish serving bugs from genuine model issues after deployment.

questions.q: According to this lesson, what is the appropriate relationship between a training team's quantization/stack suggestion and the serving team's decision-making?
options: Quantization and serving stack choices should be made randomly to avoid bias

The training team should make an evidence-based recommendation (e.g., a quantization level validated by eval delta), while the serving team retains ownership of SLAs, autoscaling, and production monitoring decisions
The serving team should ignore any input from the training team entirely
The training team should dictate the final production configuration unilaterally
questions.explain: The lesson distinguishes a recommendation, grounded in eval evidence, from a mandate. The serving team owns the production-level decisions like SLAs, autoscaling, and monitoring.

questions.q: What kind of failure does a handoff missing the validated generation config or chat template typically produce?
options: No failure at all, since generation config has no effect on output quality
A silent, hard-to-diagnose quality degradation -- the model 'feels a little off' with no easy way to tell if it's a serving bug, a formatting mismatch, or a genuine model limitation
An automatic rollback to the previous model version
A loud, immediate crash that is easy to diagnose
questions.explain: The lesson states explicitly that a handoff missing these pieces doesn't fail loudly -- it produces subtle quality issues that are difficult to attribute to a specific cause without the missing context.

questions.q: What does this lesson say comes next, now that Chapter 8 is complete?
options: The course ends here with no further lessons
A new chapter on tokenization strategies
A return to pretraining fundamentals from Chapter 2
The capstone, which brings together model selection, dataset building, fine-tuning, and evaluation from across the whole course into one end-to-end project
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly closes Chapter 8 and points to the capstone chapter, which integrates model selection, SFT dataset building, fine-tuning, and evaluation against a baseline into one hands-on project.
